stories.title: What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry
stories.summary: The post What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Regulation alone won’t fix the conditions that have earned China the reputation of the “Wild East.”

Jane Qiu is an independent science writer in Beijing.

BEIJING — In March 2023, four-year-old Mei in Shanghai was diagnosed with a rare genetic mutation linked to developmental delay and autism-like traits. Although her condition was mild and she improved with therapy and special education, her parents remained worried about her future. Hopeful for a cure, they paid Qiu Zilong, a renowned neuroscientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and his team $860,000 to develop a customized gene therapy. The treatment, which used adeno-associated viruses to deliver gene editors to the brain, had been approved by Xinhua Hospital, a leading hospital for rare diseases.

On March 24, 2025, trillions of viral particles carrying gene editors were injected into Mei’s spinal cord. She soon developed a fever and kidney failure and died within days. A year later, Qiu’s team published its preclinical findings in Nature. Mei’s case was hailed by Chinese media as “a world-class breakthrough.” Mei’s death and her family’s financial support were not mentioned.

Deaths in clinical trials are not unusual. What is shocking are the regulatory lapses revealed by an investigation published this July in Science and subsequently corroborated by a separate investigation conducted by the Shanghai municipal government, which released its findings last week. The treatment’s consent form, for instance, didn’t warn of the possibility of death. The hospital had approved treatment before toxicology findings showing liver and kidney damage in monkeys that received similar treatments. And, among other crucial omissions, the researchers failed to disclose Mei’s death.

Apparently, this was not an isolated incident. Several researchers told me that Chinese hospitals commonly fail to disclose adverse events. On Aug. 5, STAT reported another death in a gene-editing trial led by Shanghai-based HuidaGene, an incident that had remained undisclosed for about 15 months. (The Chinese team published their findings , including the fatal case, in Cell on Oct. 26.) A founder of a rare-disease organization in China told me, on condition of anonymity for fear of political repercussions, that she had encountered other trials for genetic disorders in which deaths had gone unreported. Recent revelations of undisclosed deaths in clinical trials conducted in China have prompted warnings against the use of Chinese data in U.S. drug development.

As someone who has reported on China’s ethical governance for two decades, this all feels like déjà vu. Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies — that have earned the country a reputation as biotechnology’s “Wild East.”

Back in 2006, patients flocked to China to receive unproven stem-cell therapies . When immunotherapies came into vogue a decade later, bogus advertisements for unproven interventions proliferated online until the health ministry stepped in after the high-profile death of 21-year-old student Wei Zexi. Two years later, biophysicist He Jiankui shocked the world by announcing the birth of the first genetically modified babies created using CRISPR technology.

The response in China to Mei’s death has been divided. Some netizens portray Qiu as a reckless scientist willing to gamble with patients’ lives. Others, including longtime acquaintances, describe him as a diligent scientist committed to helping patients. In some respects, Qiu represents the antithesis of He. After the CRISPR-babies scandal, Qiu openly condemned He’s reckless behavior — only to become embroiled in a comparable scandal himself six years later.

It might be tempting to blame such scandals on individual failings. The deeper questions are: What systemic factors shaped their behavior? What does the incident reveal about China’s Achilles heel in biotechnology—and about the broader culture of international science in which it is embedded? And what can the lessons teach clinical research worldwide?

Fatal Flaw

It would be unfair to suggest that China hasn’t tried to strengthen its ethical governance. The CRISPR-babies scandal prompted deep soul-searching among Chinese scholars and government officials. Since then, President Xi Jinping reportedly championed an “ethics first” approach, contrasting the “science first” mindset often seen in Chinese research. New measures have included incorporating ethics provisions in China’s first Civil Law Code, creating a national ethics committee , and enacting new ethics-review guidelines for clinical research.

But powerful forces are also pushing in the opposite direction. In 2016, China launched Healthy China 2030, making rapid application of emerging medical technologies in clinical practice a priority — not only to address unmet medical needs but to boost national competitiveness. Reforms created a new pathway to translate basic research into clinical applications for cutting-edge technologies overseen by the health ministry, alongside the conventional drug-approval route regulated by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), China’s equivalent of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This became widely known as the dual-track regulatory system.

“Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies.”

Under the technology track, clinical trials are often initiated by university researchers working with hospital clinicians rather than companies. Such investigator-initiated trials (IITs) exist worldwide. Until new regulations took effect this May, Chinese IITs were distinctive in that they could proceed with hospital approvals without the national regulatory oversight required for conventional drug trials. Compared with the NMPA route, the faster pathway allowed researchers to assess promising technologies in humans more quickly and at lower costs and help attract investment.

The result was a boom in IITs. By one estimate , more than 40,000 had been registered by April 2026, involving hundreds of thousands of participants and accounting for much of China’s translational research aimed at applying basic research to clinical practice.

China’s IIT model attracted worldwide attention. Kiran Musunuru, an expert on gene therapy at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, told me that “there is a widespread perception” that Chinese-style IITs offer a way to conduct first-in-human trials quickly and inexpensively. U.S. companies are increasingly interested in conducting IITs in China. Some U.S. researchers have even argued that the U.S should adopt elements of China’s model to accelerate drug discovery and enhance its competitiveness.

Critics, however, point to a fatal flaw: quality control. Driven by the pursuit of high-impact papers— whether for career advancement or hospital rankings — researchers rushed into first-in-human trials of emerging technologies. Hospitals are overwhelmed by proposals involving technologies with varying levels of risk. Researchers told me that as many as two dozen applications can be assessed in a single afternoon. In many cases, the process has become “a rubber-stamping exercise,” explained Zhu Wei, a bioethicist at the Shanghai Clinical Research Center.

A recent analysis of Chinese stem-cell IITs found that although a small fraction helped accelerate the application of basic research to clinical practice, most were repetitive, lacked innovation and wasted resources. Musunuru — who led the landmark development of a personalized gene-editing trial for Baby KJ, an infant with a rare life-threatening deficiency of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 that can cause dangerous ammonia buildup in the blood — warns that allowing individual hospitals to approve first-in-human trials of emerging technologies is particularly dangerous, because few researchers have sufficient experience to assess their risks. They would be “operating blind,” he told me, leaving the outcome dependent on “their appetite for risk.” That appetite can be amplified by institutional conflicts of interest. Successful trials of emerging technologies can bring researchers and hospitals fame, career advancement, high rankings and resources. Jing-Bao Nie, a bioethicist at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand, told me that these incentives can undermine institutional judgment and jeopardize patient safety. In Mei’s case, he noted, the lure of a “world-class breakthrough” may have overwhelmed necessary caution. Political interference, which is common in China, is another way the appetite for risk may outweigh caution. Chinese researchers told me that senior hospital leaders often chair the committees that review trial applications. When they seek to push through major projects led by prominent scientists, other committee members may feel unable to object. Read Noema in print. A central regulator is more insulated from such pressures and can also draw on a far broader pool of expertise. As Musumuru notes, the FDA has an army of experienced reviewers who have assessed successful and failed trials, as well as those involving serious adverse effects. Its decisions are therefore informed by “the widest possible body of knowledge,” he told me. “That’s very reassuring.” Oversight Deficiencies Zhai Xiaomei, a bioethicist at the Peking Union Medical College and a member of the national science and technology ethics committee, was not wrong when she told New Beijing News that the problems exposed by Mei’s tragedy had improved since China’s State Council Order No. 818, which established a new regulatory framework for clinical research and commercial application of cutting-edge biomedical technologies, took effect this May. Under the new rules, only top-tier hospitals can undertake IITs. Trials involving emerging technologies like gene and cell therapy, brain-machine interfaces, transplantation and microbial therapies must undergo further review by the health ministry after hospital approval. Adverse effects must be reported within five working days. Violations can result in fines, suspension or permanent ban on clinical research, loss of licenses and even criminal charges. The scientific community in China and abroad welcomes the new rules. But a researcher working closely with the ministry, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to potential career repercussions, told me that it lacks sufficient staff with the necessary technical expertise to review the large volume of applications. Consequently, the researcher added, the reviews rely heavily on experts from universities and hospitals, with only a handful assessing each case. By contrast, Musunuru told me that the U.S. FDA employs numerous in-house reviewers, many with decades of experience, and dozens pore over each submission. If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, he argues, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality. “If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality.” More troublingly, Order 818 lacks mechanisms to monitor what happens locally and identify violations. It includes neither an inspection process — a crucial component of regulatory oversight in countries such as the U.S. and UK — nor a whistleblowing platform for reporting adverse effects and deaths. Such mechanisms are particularly important in countries where transparency is limited, and the press is not free. Without them, violations may go unnoticed and the penalties risk becoming little more than empty threats. Researchers, like bioethicist Ma Yonghui of Xiamen University, also worry that regulatory exemptions could create loopholes. Military hospitals, for instance, fall outside health ministry rules. The two dozen or so free trade zones across China, particularly in Bo’ao on the tropical island of Hainan, may enjoy special regulatory treatment, potentially attracting foreign researchers and companies seeking to conduct ethically contentious trials they could not undertake in their own countries. There are ample precedents of scientists exploiting countries with weak ethics governance as sites for risky research. In October 2018, one month before the CRISPR-babies scandal, He and John Zhang, founder and medical director of the New Hope Fertility Center in New York City, met Hainan’s vice governor to discuss establishing a clinic in Bo’ao to offer experimental procedures, including heritable genome editing. Zhang had already attracted international attention in 2016 for helping produce in Mexico the world’s first “three-parent baby” to prevent the transmission of mitochondrial DNA mutations from the mother. The procedure involved replacing faulty mitochondria with healthy ones from a female donor during in vitro fertilization, a procedure that was — and still is — illegal in the U.S. Hype & Hope While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations, Nie told me. The case offers a window into people’s relationship with biotechnology in China as well as their hopes and expectations — shaped not only by scientists but by society at large. Over the past decade, rare-disease advocacy organizations have grown rapidly in China, helping improve patient care, pressing for government support and driving research through collecting genetic data, studying disease progression and funding clinical trials. Su Yeyang, an independent anthropologist in Langfang in Hebei province who works with rare-disease communities, told me this has given families a sense of agency. With limited social support and a market-driven drug-discovery model that has failed rare-disease communities worldwide, they are doing whatever they can “to help themselves, their children and their community,” she said. With gene therapy, the “magic cure” long hoped for by many rare-disease patients seems within reach. In one high-profile case, a fledgling company approached Xu Wei, a high-school graduate in his 30s in Kunming, in China’s southern province of Yunnan, to develop a gene therapy for his son. The boy had Menkes syndrome, a rare genetic disorder that impairs copper absorption and causes developmental delays and premature death. The company, with no track record in neurodevelopmental diseases, claimed to have developed the treatment in less than a year. In 2022, the 3-year-old received it at a private hospital in a trial that, based on publicly available accounts, appeared not to include biomarker or behavioral assessments of efficacy. Chinese media reported enthusiastically on anecdotal claims of improvements while downplaying the risks of undertaking such experimental therapies. A patient advocacy leader told me such cases are not uncommon in China, where at least 20 million people are living with rare diseases. They offer hope, whether grounded in evidence or not, and can encourage others to follow. “We try to explain to families that pouring millions into a trial is no guarantee of success” and could even backfire, she says. Even well-educated parents, like Mei’s, may underestimate the complexity of clinical research and overestimate what experimental therapies can achieve. It’s unclear whether Qiu, who was fired by the university last week and barred from participating in scientific research for five years following the government investigation , helped foster such expectations. He has not publicly given his account. But his book, “ The Autism Enlightenment ,” published this April, was revealing. It recounted how, in 2010, he told the mother of a child with Rett syndrome — a rare, genetic neurodevelopmental disorder leading to severe cognitive and physical impairments — that a cure would likely emerge in three to five years. It did not discuss fatal risks often associated with first-in-human trials. It did not mention Jessie Gelsinger, who had a mild form of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, a condition that can lead to abnormally high levels of ammonia in the blood and died in 1999 from a preventable complication of an experimental gene therapy. “While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations.” Gelsinger was the first person publicly identified as having died in a gene therapy clinical trial, which undermined public trust in the field and set back its progress for decades. Nor did the book draw caution from the death in 2024 of a girl with Rett syndrome in the first brain-directed gene therapy for the condition. In both cases, scientists used the same type of virus as Qiu did. In a society where disability and genetic disease remain stigmatized, and families receive limited support, Mei’s parents placed their hopes in Qiu and gene editing. Like the couple who turned to He Jiankui to protect their children from HIV and the associated discrimination by editing their embryos, they sought a technological solution to social problems. As the Illness Challenge Foundation, a Beijing-based rare-disease advocacy organization, put it after Mei’s death , “responsible innovation should not entice patients to stake their lives in the name of hope.” China’s Gelsinger Moment? Gelsinger’s death in 1999 was a game changer. It’s widely regarded as a cautionary tale of how a toxic combination of scientific hype and insufficient safeguards can jeopardize patient safety. It triggered institutional reforms and significant changes in research culture in the U.S. that were aimed at rebuilding public and regulatory trust. Mei’s death could be China’s Gelsinger moment. It has exposed regulatory failings, a scientific ethos that encourages hype and recklessness, and deeper societal problems surrounding disability and genetic disease. None is unique to China, but they are particularly acute in a country facing a distinctive combination of political and developmental challenges. At the heart of the incident lies the “moral arbitrage” of experimental therapies, a recurrent theme in biotechnological innovation worldwide. On one hand, patients want access to cutting-edge, unproven treatments when they see them as their only hope. On the other hand, such treatments carry risks, which often accompany medical breakthroughs. Navigating the contours between hope and risk requires more than scientific evidence and regulatory rules, Su told me. It demands critical reflection on the culture of international science that places a premium on competition, sensational research, and being first at any cost. It also calls for broader societal dialogues about the diverse notions of human flourishing, the stigmatization of disabilities, and the need for greater support for people living with rare diseases. If China can learn from the failures and undertake the regulatory, scientific and social reforms needed to address its biotech governance failures — and if the rest of the world can look beyond the country’s small number of success stories out of a hidden ocean of low-quality and potentially harmful clinical trials — Mei’s death will not have been in vain. stories.body:
A Catholic priest offers a blessing on the shores of Lake Victoria. Priests perform rituals at landing sites, praying for bountiful catches at an increasingly unpredictable time.

PHOTO ESSAY

The largest tropical lake on Earth, Africa’s Lake Victoria is under enormous strain, with its waters contaminated, fisheries decimated, and shorelines drowning. The losses have spurred renewed calls to protect the lake, which supports more than 45 million people across the region.

By Matilde Gattoni and Matteo Fagotto • November 19, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

Lake Victoria, the largest tropical lake on Earth, is under enormous strain as overfishing, pollution, and a changing climate are decimating its fisheries, contaminating its waters, and bringing record floods to its shores. The losses have spurred renewed calls to protect the lake, whose basin supports more than 45 million people across the region.

For decades, Lake Victoria’s fishing industry relied on bountiful catches of Nile tilapia and Nile perch, both introduced to the lake in the 1950s. The perch, a voracious predator blamed for the disappearance of some 200 native cichlid species, became the lake’s most lucrative prize, with its filets exported to Europe and the Middle East. In recent years, overfishing has dramatically reduced fish stocks, including perch, pushing many fishermen to use illegal fine-mesh nets that catch juvenile fish before they can reproduce. Kenya’s catch fell from 94,349 metric tons in 2021 to 70,231 metric tons in 2025, according to the country’s fisheries service. In Uganda, the number of plants processing Nile perch has dropped from 21 to six, according to the director of operations at Victoria Treasures, one of the few surviving factories.

Pollution from farms, gold mining, and booming shoreline cities — including Kampala, Uganda’s capital, and Mwanza, Tanzania’s second-largest city — has compounded the damage as untreated sewage and fertilizers feed recurring algal blooms and water hyacinth invasions, which starve the water of oxygen and suffocate fish.

Yale Environment 360 / Created with Datawrapper

Making matters worse, exceptional rains linked with climate change lifted the lake to record levels in 2020 and again in 2024. The floods have forced hundreds of thousands of people from their homes and swallowed farmland and fish landing sites. The World Meteorological Organization expects this year’s El Niño, which typically brings heavier rains to East Africa, to last into 2027, raising the risk of further displacement.

In July, during the UNESCO World Heritage Committee meeting in Busan, South Korea, more than 100 civil society groups from 35 countries proposed recognizing Lake Victoria as a living cultural landscape, based on the fishing knowledge, rituals, and oral traditions its lakeside communities have accumulated over generations. The groups insisted that any nomination should protect local communities from displacement and safeguard the livelihoods of both fishers and the women who sell their catch.

If approved, inscription on the World Heritage list could bring international attention, technical help, and limited funding. It would also commit the governments of Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania to protecting the lake under an agreed management plan.

Photographer Matilde Gattoni spent February and March on Lake Victoria’s Kenyan, Ugandan, and Tanzanian shores. This photo essay combines images that reflect the lake’s dire condition — from the water hyacinths that clog landing sites to the residents displaced by floods — with images that speak to the countless ties, both economic and spiritual, that continue to bind the people to the lake.

Scroll down to see the images, or click on the photo below to launch a slideshow.

Invasive water hyacinth in Ogenya, Kenya, robs the lake of dissolved oxygen and blocks sunlight from penetrating the water. The weed, pushed by the wind into shallow areas, also keeps fishermen from reaching open water.

In Sindo, Kenya, women working as fishmongers vie for a piece of a dwindling catch. The competition has led to jaboya , or “sex for fish”: Women must trade sexual favors with fishermen to secure enough product to provide for their families.

Joyce Akinyi Odiko, 53, began as a fish seller but eventually assembled her own fleet of 30 boats, becoming one of the few women on the lake to own what she catches. As fisheries collapse in Uhanya, Kenya, she is considering selling her boats and leaving fishing behind.

A trader sells omena and fried fish in the largest market in Kisumu, Kenya. Populations of omena have plummeted as a result of overfishing and warming that is reducing oxygen levels in the lake.

A young woman in Uhanya, Kenya, wades through the submerged ruins of a communal fish processing site. In many coastal villages, floods have swallowed infrastructure, displaced residents, and moved the shoreline hundreds of feet inland.

Rising lake levels destroyed the mud and log home of Jane Anyango Okelo, in Ogenya. When the water receded it left behind highly fertile soil for crops, but Jane and her husband can’t afford to rebuild their home and now live in a makeshift tent.

A girl eats her only meal of the day in an alley of the informal camp at the Kigungu landing site in Uganda. Most of the people here are refugees from Makusa and Lwamunyo islands, which were almost entirely submerged by floods in 2020.

Many fishermen have turned to sand mining in nearby river mouths as fish stocks have shrunk. The practice is illegal as dredging destroys vital fish breeding grounds, disturbs the habitats of hippos and crocodiles, and leads to the erosion of wetlands.

A laborer carries a massive bundle of rice hay on his back after the harvest in Nduru, Kenya. Fertilizer runoff from farms in the region flows directly into the nearby Nyando River and into Lake Victoria, fueling the growth of invasive water hyacinth that chokes the shoreline.

Mercury used in informal and largely unregulated gold mining operations in Macalder, Kenya, can spill into rivers that eventually discharge into Lake Victoria.

A young girl in Kigungu examines a freshly caught Nile perch. Stocks of the highly profitable fish have dwindled, so processing companies now hire agents to scour landing sites and rush large specimens to factories for export.

stories.title: Scouts say they face £1m tourist tax cost for overnight trips
stories.summary: The increased cost after the proposed Visitors Levy is imposed could price some young people out of joining Scout camps and other trips, the group said.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 21 November 2026, 12:53 GMT

Scout groups are warning they could face an additional annual bill of £1m as a result of the government's proposed tourist tax for England.

The overnight levy would allow councils and regional authorities to charge visitors an additional fee for their accommodation, including campsites, raising money to be spent on local services.

The increased cost from the Visitors Levy could price some young people out of joining Scout camps and other trips, the group said.

Dwayne Fields, the UK's Chief Scout, has called for youth groups to be exempted and said the charity - which sees more than 1.4m overnight stays a year - would be "firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations".

The Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government told the BBC that local leaders who introduce the levy "will have the option to exempt certain types of accommodation in their areas, including accommodation which is often used for trips by youth groups like Scouts and Girl Guides - such as camping pitches".

They added money raised from the levy will "stay local and be invested in the visitor experience and local growth including in high streets, parks and events".

Labour mayors have indicated they would cap the levy at 5% but the legislation contains no maximum limit.

In a statement, the Scout Association said the tax, if set at 5% across the country, could cost the charity £1.04m a year and force volunteers to deal with onerous paperwork.

They worked this out by assuming the levy would be set at 5% for all the 1,423,344 annual overnight stays across Squirrels, Beavers, Cubs, Scouts, Explorers and volunteers.

Girlguiding would also be subject to the levy.

In a statement, Fields said: "We strongly support investment being made available to strengthen local communities. Well-crafted legislation can unlock that opportunity.

"But we are firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations for camping trips that equip young people with skills for life, while burdening volunteers with the role of unpaid government tax collectors."

Manchester Scout volunteer Chris Taylor called the proposals "madness"

Chris Taylor, lead volunteer for Greater Manchester East Scout County, called the levy a "tent tax" and branded it "madness".

Referring to the levy being applied to the Linnet Clough campsite run by his group in Stockport, he said: "Our members spent nearly 25,000 nights away from home last year, and a 5% levy would add over £11,000 a year to the cost of their camps and sleepovers."

He added: "On top of that, and as a charity, we'd have to employ someone just to collect the tax and send returns to the Mayor's office. That's another £7,000 a year, and that's just one campsite - there are plenty more across Manchester."

Labour MP Gareth Snell, who challenged ministers when the levy was debated in the House of Commons , said Scouts "provide some of the most memorable experiences for young people up and down the country."

The Stoke-on-Trent Central MP called on the government to take the decision out of mayors' hands and ensure Scout camps are exempted from the bill.

The Welsh Government has announced young people staying in hostels, campsites or outdoor centres would be exempt from its tourism tax, due to come into effect next year.

stories.summary: Brussels sources had previously suggested the bloc might not apply the wider deal until fees were lowered for EU students in Britain.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:

Watch: Miliband spoke to the BBC following the summit in Brussels

Published 21 November 2026, 06:00 GMT

A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.

The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a new youth mobility scheme.

However, a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "confident" a solution would be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding "me too" during a press conference announcing the deal.

Meanwhile, asked in his interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether rejoining the EU would be looked at, Miliband said "all the options will be on the table".

It came after the prime minister said that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.

What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start? Published 1 day ago

Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more Published 1 day ago

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow Published 1 day ago

UK and EU leaders have hailed the closer cooperation agreement, with Burnham calling the deal a "win-win" that could lower the cost of living and reduce red tape.

The prime minister said the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.

EU sources had earlier suggested that the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.

Miliband said it was "absolutely clear" the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.

"President von der Leyen... was very clear about this at the press conference we just had. She said there are those three agreements and then there's a separate piece of paper and a separate issue, which is looking at the issue of tuition," he said.

Asked again whether the agreements would definitely become law, the foreign secretary said: "Yes, absolutely."

"The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we're introducing legislation in Parliament, so definitely."

Miliband said there would be "no cost" to the UK taxpayer for anything agreed at Friday's summit, adding that there would be no new contributions to the EU budget.

He said previously announced agreements on EU schemes like Erasmus+ were a "separate decision" and the summit "was not about cost to the taxpayer".

Speaking on Friday, Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

Miliband told the BBC that "of course all the options will be on the table" when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding that "we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options".

He said that while he accepted the result of the 2016 Brexit referendum, "the world has changed massively".

"Europe is changing too, so we've got to look at what that means. It's not about this parliament, we're respecting the red lines in this parliament," he added.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was "not fair", arguing that UK farmers would have to follow rules set in Brussels and young people from the EU would "compete" with young Britons struggling to get jobs at home.

She also claimed Burnham had "plucked" the £17bn figure out of thin air, and said the only modelling she had seen of how the agreement could boost the economy put the figure at "0.0%".

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said Friday marked a "betrayal of the British people" and a good day for the EU to "try and humiliate" the UK.

Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, wrote on social media: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.

"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, the University of Manchester's vice chancellor Professor Duncan Ivison said closer UK-EU relations were a "good thing" but "the issue of tuition fees is something we do have to figure out because there is a cost".

He warned that EU students being allowed to pay domestic university fees would "take £500m, we estimate, out of the higher education sector at a time where there's a lot of pressure on the sector".

He added: "If EU students come and are paying domestic fees, it's not clear we'd be able to increase the number of places for EU students anyway."

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said the Treasury and Department for Education would work with universities to find a solution during negotiations.

She told BBC Breakfast: "I don't think anybody wants to do deals that negatively impact anything. We want win-win deals."

stories.body:
The US president rated his summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin as 12 out of 10 but China and Russia had the most to celebrate

H e got by with a little help from his friends. Rebuked by millions of voters in a still resilient democracy, Donald Trump travelled to Asia this week and found comfort in the company of autocrats who still flatter him.

The US president, reduced to lame-duck status at home by a humiliating midterm election defeat, returned to the global stage in a meeting with two strongmen in Shenzhen, China, that critics described as a new low for America’s claim to moral authority.

“ Who is he? ” Trump asked rhetorically, pointing as he walked towards the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin. “He’s my friend.” Separately he told the Chinese president, Xi Jinping: “You’re my friend, and we have a very special relationship.”

Trump, Xi and Putin convened at the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, China, for the first-ever trilateral summit among the leaders of the US, China and Russia, the world’s three biggest nuclear powers. The official product of their 70-minute closed-door meeting was a four-point document titled the “Declaration Toward Peace” that made no mention of the wars in Iran or Ukraine.

But the defining image was of the trio sitting around a huge circular wooden table. At its hollow centre sat an immaculate arrangement of pink flowers, an ancient Chinese motif meant to evoke harmony. To US-based critics, however, the optics sent a different signal.

Steve Schmidt , a former adviser to George W Bush and John McCain, said: “The image of the grotesque large round table with a war criminal dictator, a stable dictator and an irrational, delusional wannabe dictator is an image of deep shame and weakness for the United States.

“It’s a repudiation of American values, American honour, common sense and the national security interests of the country, and a betrayal of America’s allies all across the world.”

Beijing understood how to satisfy the Trump ego. When Air Force One landed in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, Xi made the unusual move of greeting Trump personally on the tarmac. An honour guard stood at attention, crowds waved miniature US and Chinese flags, schoolchildren shook pompoms and Xi drew Trump into a warm embrace.

Trump took the bait with delight. For him, victory was not measured in negotiating concessions but in the lavish banquet and the seat reserved for him at the head table. “That’s a big win for us,” he said in a TV interview. “It’s a big win for China too. We get along.” Trump was even treated to a performance of YMCA, the signature song of his campaign rallies.

In their first meeting since failed negotiations in Alaska last year, Trump held one-on-one talks with Putin that touched on Ukraine but secured no immediate commitments. The meeting occurred against a backdrop of Trump recently rejecting new sanctions on Russia.

In a bilateral meeting with Xi, Trump raised the US-led war in Iran, emphasising a joint interest in fully reopening the strait of Hormuz and preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons. Xi focused on US-China trade stability and asserted China’s sovereign position on Taiwan, treating it as an unalterable domestic issue.

In one ominous remark, Trump told Xi: “I think as long as you and I are in charge of things, we’ll never have a problem.” He later told NBC News that the pair had also agreed that artificial intelligence needed some form of safety “guardrails” but offered few details.

The main event was the trilateral summit, with observers watching body language closely for any clues about the dynamics among Xi, relishing his role as host, Putin, whose war in Ukraine is faltering, and Trump, ostensibly the most powerful of the three but politically wounded at home. To many, it offered little more than a glorified photo op.

Brett Bruen , the president of the public affairs agency Global Situation Room and the former global engagement director of the Barack Obama White House, said: “Brand Trump has been badly sullied by a historic defeat at the hands of American voters. However, this isn’t going to improve his standing internationally and certainly not domestically.

“If anything, it put on display his desperation. It put on display his isolation internationally from the very people that he’s going to need to be able to secure trade deals or peace deals. Once again he’s returning from China with the luggage hold empty of any diplomatic accomplishments.”

The formal output of the summit was a study in profound omissions and authoritarian wishlists. The text made no mention of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, nor of the spiralling US military conflict with Iran.

Instead, the trio agreed on four broad points: pledging dialogue to reduce nuclear risks, committing to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum, calling for “reforms” to the United Nations and declaring that state sovereignty and the immunity of state officials must be respected while warning that the international criminal court (ICC) must not abuse its jurisdiction.

Putin currently faces an active ICC arrest warrant for war crimes in Ukraine, while the Trump administration has sanctioned ICC officials to shield itself and its ally Israel from judicial scrutiny.

Ned Price , a former deputy to the US representative to the UN, said: “The joint statement was notable, not because Russia and China said it, but because the United States also co-signed.

“The United Nations they want is not a United Nations that’s more effective but rather a United Nations that is less effective at upholding the rules of the road, the very principles that have been at the centre of the UN system since its founding: the idea that big countries can’t bully small countries, that borders can’t be redrawn by force.”

The talks have done little to dispel the impression that Trump regards Congress, the media and elections as pesky encumbrances while gazing with awe and some envy at Xi and Putin. As the Shenzhen summit concluded, European leaders and Nato officials convened urgently in Berlin to reinforce their support for Ukraine and resist any high-level partitioning of European security.

The summit was a propaganda win for Putin, who went from international pariah status to equal billing with the world’s two biggest economies. It was also a victory for Xi. Without making any concessions on Taiwan, trade tariffs or its industrial lifeline to Moscow, China positioned itself as the arbiter of 21st-century diplomacy.

“Xi was able to burnish China’s diplomatic sway and give Putin and Trump something that each leader respectively coveted,” said Ali Wyne , senior research and advocacy adviser for US-China relations at the International Crisis Group. “He gave Putin the opportunity to demonstrate that despite Russia’s wartime losses, despite western sanctions, Russia remains a great power.

“He gave Trump the opportunity to demonstrate, at least in Trump’s own mind, that despite these bruising midterm elections, Trump is a singularly visionary and consequential peacemaker, thereby appealing to Trump’s ego.”

While neither Beijing nor Moscow harbours any illusions about Trump’s volatile temperament, both recognise the ticking clock on his second term and know they are likely to outlast him.

Wyne added: “Both of them recognise that it is next to impossible that any of President Trump’s successors will view them in comparable terms as friends, adopt conciliatory dispositions, and on certain issues come close to aligning US positions with those of China and Russia.”

Although he was caught on camera apparently nodding off, Trump departed China appearing politically rejuvenated after his encounters with his two “friends”. He hailed the visit as “Highly Consequential” on social media and said later: “On a scale of zero to 10, I think it was a 12.”

stories.title: Staff gagging clauses lifted ahead of probe into culture at data watchdog
stories.summary: Ministers are expected to publish the details of how an independent review of the working environment at the Information Commission will be carried out next week.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 21 November 2026, 06:01 GMT

Non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) signed by staff at the UK's information watchdog will be lifted to allow them to speak out about its culture, the government has confirmed.

Ministers are expected to publish the details of how an independent review of the working environment at the Information Commission will be carried out next week.

It follows the departure of the watchdog's boss five months ago amid allegations of sexually inappropriate behaviour.

A government spokesperson confirmed that NDAs, known as "gagging clauses", would not be enforced by the Information Commission, saying the regulator "will not use the terms of any agreement to prevent people from participating in the review".

The government "will set out further details on the review, including its terms of reference and the independent reviewer, shortly", they added.

The Information Commission is one of the UK's most high-profile regulators charged with the crucial task of regulating AI, data protection and Freedom of Information requests.

It recently won a court battle with TikTok after it fined the social media platform £12.7m for misusing children's data, and has penalised bodies including the Ministry of Defence after an email blunder exposed the details of interpreters fleeing Afghanistan.

But it has been without permanent leadership since Information Commissioner John Edwards resigned earlier this year .

It came after an independent investigation found a "case to answer" over reports of alleged inappropriate behaviour towards staff including claims of sexual harassment.

The Information Commission said the investigation found Edwards' behaviour "fell short of the conduct expected from a public official".

In a resignation statement posted on his LinkedIn page in June, Edwards said he disagreed with how the investigation had been carried out but accepted his position had "become untenable".

The statement continued: "I have accepted that there have been occasions where I exercised poor judgement and made attempts at humour that were inappropriate and caused offence."

Freedom of Information requests have found that since the start of Edwards' tenure in 2022 to the present, 16 current and former employees have signed non-disclosure or confidentiality clauses costing more than £354,000.

Nine of those , external included a "non-derogatory clause" which legally prevents employees from making negative comments publicly.

While this is a small proportion of the more than 1,000 staff employed by the commissioner, government advice stipulates that public bodies should only use confidentiality clauses "when necessary" and that they should "not seek to stifle or discourage staff from raising concerns".

Since 2025, new laws also mean they cannot be used to silence employees subjected to harassment or abuse.

After Edwards' departure, the government announced a review , external into the Commission's culture and governance, with the then-Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology Liz Kendall telling a committee of MPs she was "absolutely appalled at what the independent investigator found - sexual harassment and bullying".

Five months later, the investigation has not begun.

In recent weeks, the two major civil service unions, the PCS and FDA, have pushed for an external examination of the events leading up to Edwards' resignation in meetings with government officials.

The unions have also asked for those who signed non-disclosure agreements with the ICO to be released from them so they can contribute to the review.

The PCS union says other concerns had previously been raised with them about Edwards, including a bullying complaint, which was investigated at the time.

An internal staff survey, published in August and released under FOI , external points towards wider issues at the Commission, with 14% of all employees reporting they had either personally experienced bullying, harassment and discrimination.

Multiple current and former employees have also told the BBC of experiencing or witnessing incidents of bullying or harassment.

PCS General Secretary Fran Heathcote said the union's members at the Commission "have been failed for too long by a toxic leadership culture that has allowed bullying and harassment to persist, leaving many staff fearful of speaking out".

Heathcote said she welcomed the "positive engagement" the union had received in recent weeks from the Commission and officials at the Department for Culture Media and Sport (DCMS), which oversees it.

But she added: "For the review to command the confidence of staff, it must be genuinely independent, robust in its approach, and prepared to identify where accountability lies."

Conservative MP Caroline Dinenage, who chairs the DCMS select committee, said the Commission "needed a firm new direction" after the departure of its former boss.

"Instead, a leadership vacuum has compounded what went before at a rudderless organisation where it seems the worst behaviours in the workplace are not being challenged," she added.

She said it was "vital" the government brought in "someone who can set a new tone and is dedicated to changing attitudes and protecting staff" to head up the Commission.

A spokesperson for the Information Commission said its commitment to an independent review reflected its "ongoing commitment to listening and learning from the events of the past year and those leading up to it".

"Our new Board, appointed this summer, has been working exceptionally hard to provide fresh leadership, ushering in a new governance structure and a new strategy," they added.

"It is committed to listening carefully to the review's findings and recommendations, and building on the positive work on our culture already taking place across the organisation."

stories.body:
UK economy defies City predictions and Iran war fallout, with gap between spending and income about £1bn lower than expected in October, at £17bn

The UK government borrowed less than expected in October despite a rise in debt interest costs, in a boost for chancellor John Healey amid the pressure on Britain’s economy from the Middle East war.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said public sector net borrowing – the difference between government spending and income – was £17bn in October, about £800m higher than the same month a year ago. City economists had forecast borrowing would increase by more, to £18bn.

In the financial year so far, public sector net borrowing was £111.3bn, the ONS said – £7.3bn less than in the same period last year, helped by stronger tax receipts.

The Office for Budget Responsibility, the independent Treasury watchdog, said the latest figures were “broadly in line” with its October forecast for a £1.1bn fall in total borrowing for the 2026-27 financial year. However, it warned there were “several risks” amid the sharp rise in energy costs, and public spending on cost of living support measures.

Grant Fitzner, the ONS chief economist, said: “Borrowing so far this financial year remained lower than in the same period last year with receipts growing faster than spending. Income-related taxes’ receipts grew particularly strongly.

“However, monthly borrowing was up on last October, partly down to higher debt interest.”

The latest figures showed rising borrowing costs on financial markets drove the UK’s debt interest payments to £11.2bn in October – £2.8bn more than in the same month last year, and the highest figure for any October since monthly records began in 1997.

Some government bonds are directly linked to the retail prices index measure of inflation, with payments rising in line with it. RPI has increased in recent months as the Iran war has pushed up energy costs.

Public sector net debt rose to £3.1tn, equivalent to 95.8% of GDP – 1.9 percentage points higher than last year and at levels last seen in the early 1960s.

Chief secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, said Britain was showing “standout resilience despite the global impact of the conflict in Iran.

“This year we’ve cut borrowing faster than any other G20 country. Now we’re going to cut waste and bureaucracy by reprioritising spending and making public services more efficient with AI,” Reynolds added.

Britain’s economy has continued to grow at the second-fastest rate in the G7 despite the fallout from the war in the Middle East, bolstered by AI investment and households continuing to spend.

In his budget last month, Healey raised taxes on banks to fund relief for households being squeezed by the energy shock from the Middle East war.

after newsletter promotion

Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, Healey stuck to the government’s fiscal rules with £15bn of headroom – less than the £23.6bn buffer left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, as the conflict drove up the UK government’s borrowing costs.

After a low-key budget statement designed with febrile bond markets in mind, economists warned the chancellor had set himself up for a “brutal” spending review next year.

Avoiding a return to austerity for unprotected government departments could require a £17bn top-up to the spending plans for 2030-31, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies. That is before taking into account an additional £11bn needed to fund a commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP.

Official figures on Wednesday showed inflation in the UK rose in October to 3.6% amid the global surge in energy prices triggered by the Iran war. Economic forecasters predict a further rise in inflation, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak of close to 5% next year.

Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month and warned further increases might be required to combat inflationary pressures unleashed by the Iran war. Financial markets predict three quarter-point rate increases before the end of next year.

Rob Wood, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics, said: “The October budget did little to address the more serious challenges facing the public finances, so we continue to have doubts about the government’s ability to follow through on its fiscal plans, suggesting upside risks to borrowing in the coming years.”

stories.body:
State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors

California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.

Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.

“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.

“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: companies cannot mislead their investors.”

The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.

Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China .

Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.

Bonta said the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.

“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he said. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”

Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.

Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, said the company had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back .

Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.

after newsletter promotion

Shares in rival chipmaker AMD closed down almost 8% on Thursday after the publication of reports connected to short seller Hunterbrook warning about its links to China and the “circular financing” of customers.

The company, which has been targeted amid the Nvidia scandal, is looking at a further fall of more than 5% in pre-market trading.

Hunterbrook Media published allegations on the use of AMD’s software by a Chinese server maker blacklisted by the US. Sister publication, The Bear Cave newsletter, alleged that AMD’s use of datacentre lease guarantees and backstops for unsold cloud computing capacity could leave it exposed to a pullback in AI spending.

AMD said the reports’ claims “misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships”.

“AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” the company said. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.”

AMD’s share price has more than doubled so far this year, giving the company a market capitalisation of more than $800m.

stories.body:
Comments come after the leaders met on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen, China

Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast

Xi Jinping says a “full turnaround” has been achieved in Australia-China relations, praising Anthony Albanese as the pair met in Shenzhen on Friday.

The two leaders held talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, as the federal government continues efforts to stabilise trade and security relations with Beijing after a rocky period under the former Coalition government.

Beijing launched a punishing round of trade tariffs after efforts by Australia to keep Chinese telecommunications firm Huawei from taking part in the rollout of 5G mobile services – and after calls from the Morrison government for a full international investigation in the origins of the Covid-19 pandemic.

About $20bn in tariffs were added to key Australian exports, including barley, wine, beef, lobsters, coal and timber.

But, after an intense diplomatic campaign and the lifting of many of the tariffs, the Australian leader received a warm welcome from Xi on Friday.

He welcomed Albanese at Kylin Villa, the sprawling complex where he hosted US president, Donald Trump, and Russian president, Vladimir Putin, a day earlier.

“China-Australia friendship is what the people want,” Xi said.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

He nodded appreciatively when Albanese said he had first visited Shenzhen in the late 1990s and described the “remarkable” development in the city that “embodies the rise and growth of China”.

As media were ushered from the room Xi called Albanese a “China hand” because he’d visited the country so many times.

“Since you became prime minister in 2022, we have had four meetings,” Xi said.

“We have jointly promoted the full turnaround of China-Australia relations, and exchanges and cooperation in various fields between our two countries have continued to deepen.”

In prepared remarks, Xi told Albanese he would work to advance ties between Beijing and Canberra.

“I will work with you in the spirit of equality, seeking common ground despite differences, and mutually beneficial cooperation to take forward the China-Australia Comprehensive Strategic Partnership,” he said.

Albanese said the relationship “delivers prosperity” for both countries.

“The relationship that we are building is positive, is calm, is not defined by our differences, but one where we can have clear and frank exchanges for our mutual interest,” he said.

The talks come at the end of an 11-day diplomatic trip which has included the Asean and Apec summits , the Cop31 climate talks and a meeting of the Quad leaders in Manila.

Albanese said before the talks that he would explain new planned joint military exercises with the US, Japan and India, as well as the federal government’s determination to terminate Chinese company Landbridge’s 99-year lease on the Port of Darwin.

That promise, made before the 2025 election, has become bogged down in international legal action.

Albanese pledged to raise a wide range of issues in the bilateral relationship, which Labor has worked hard to stabilise since coming to office in 2022. Greater market access for Australian beef producers remains an outstanding priority for the government, with 55% tariffs in place due to China’s quota system.

Officials expected Xi to raise concerns about Australia cooperation on AI and defence with Washington, and a new critical minerals agreement signed with the Trump administration.

Before leaving for his return to Australia, Albanese flew to Beijing for a formal meeting with the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, and for an Australia-China business summit.

The two leaders agreed to a new AI dialogue, on safety, governance and application, and agreed 2027 would be the Australia-China Year of Tourism.

Albanese praised the “understanding and trust” in the relationship.

“You are rather wise in speaking about the turbulent seas that are there in international relations,” he said.

“In those circumstances us navigating those turbulent seas but keeping our eyes on the horizon, means that our relationship can bloom like the flowers that are in front of us here,” he continued, gesturing to the lavender flowers in between the tables.

stories.title: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
stories.summary: The UK-EU deal agreed on Friday covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa join hands at the end of a press conference during the EU-UK summit in Brussels

Published 20 November 2026

Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.

European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".

Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.

Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.

The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.

This video can not be played

Watch: What the new UK-EU deal could mean for European relations

The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.

The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.

A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.

There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too."

On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.

Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".

The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Watch: Will the UK-EU summit deal boost the economy?

'Brainstorming process'

Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."

The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.

Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".

He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.

Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.

"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."

Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.

The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.

Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".

'Endless betrayal'

Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".

Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".

She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".

Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."

In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.

"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

stories.title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
stories.summary: The trade deal is unlikely lower food prices for shoppers, but should boost the economy more than other post-Brexit agreements.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 20 November 2026

The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.

In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.

And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.

The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".

Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".

Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?

This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.

This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry.

However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced.

No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports.

Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape.

In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market.

But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports.

The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040.

Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation.

The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes.

The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale.

Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people".

Bringing all the agreements on food, emissions and the youth experience together, the economy is forecast to get an overall boost of 0.5%, or £17bn a year.

A modest boost, but high by the standards of past post-Brexit trade deals, for example, with Australia, India or Japan and the Gulf and the trans-pacific deal.

This UK-EU pact actually matches all of those agreements combined for expected growth measured by the Treasury's own assessments.

The biggest single boost to the overall economy would come from more European young workers. However, the economy benefit of this part of the deal per person reduces to zero, according to the government's own calculations.

Burham also said he hoped a planned electricity deal with the EU would cut bills, but that has not been done yet, and requires a contribution into the bloc's budget for poorer regions.

The electricity deal could help lower bills, but that contains a clear trade-off.

There are still some details to be revealed in the full legal texts of these documents.

The bigger point is whether this logic of gaining free-flowing access for food, in exchange for giving up regulatory freedom, will now apply elsewhere.

Is food now a blueprint for future negotiations? It had been the Starmer-Rachel Reeves strategy to spread this model to other sectors such as cars, and chemicals.

The big takeaway from today was that both the PM and his counterparts publicly acknowledged the end of the incremental piecemeal approach to aligning with the single market.

The question is whether the PM thinks what goes for food applies across the whole economy. Most economists predict that could lead to much bigger economic gains, but it will also be a much bigger constitutional battle.

stories.title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?
stories.summary: The agreement will allow young people between 18 and 31 year-olds to travel, work or study in the EU for up to three years.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 20 November 2026

The UK and EU have agreed a youth experience scheme which will allow a limited number of 18 to 31-year-olds to work, study or travel in the European Union for up to three years.

Every year, 100,000 Britons will be able to participate in the scheme, with a reciprocal arrangement for 100,000 EU citizens.

A joint EU-UK statement says the scheme is due to launch no later than January 2030.

The numbers for both those coming to and from the EU will be allocated among the member nations according to each country's population.

UK participants will initially be able to apply to travel to one particular EU country but can later switch to a different one, staying in a total of three countries during their three-year stay. However, they must spend 12 months in one country before switching.

Visas issued by the EU or the UK will initially be valid for two years, with an option to extend for one more year.

Neither UK nor EU citizens will be able to access benefits while abroad or bring dependants such as children.

Participants will need to pay an application fee and prove they have enough money to support themselves during their stay.

There are currently no details on what application fees UK citizens will have to pay, but the EU currently charges €90 (£75) for short-term visas. Numbers vary between countries for longer-term stays.

The UK charges £340 for its other youth mobility schemes, in addition to a £776 annual health surcharge.

The UK government has not said how much money an EU or UK national needs to have access to in order to take part but for similar schemes the figure is £2,530.

There are no details yet on how places on the scheme will be allocated if it is oversubscribed; however previous schemes have used either a first-come, first-served basis or a random ballot system.

The UK already has youth mobility schemes in place with other countries, including 45,000 places for Australians, 8,500 for New Zealanders and 1,000 for Icelanders.

In 2024, 24,400 out of a possible total of 81,100 youth mobility scheme visas were issued by the UK.

Speaking at a joint press conference with EU leaders, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "These opportunities open horizons, and they create friendships that will last a lifetime.

"So it's a very emotional moment because these are the young people that will shape our future."

What about tuition fees?

One sticking point in the negotiations had been tuition fees and the EU's request that Europeans studying at UK universities should pay the same as British students.

A typical undergraduate degree in the UK (excluding Scotland) costs up to £9,790 a year for a domestic student, while the cost for international students, including those from the EU, can vary from around £11,000 to £38,000.

If the UK did agree to reduce fees for EU students, British higher education institutions could lose out financially.

British students at European institutions pay non-EU rates, but these tend to be lower than in the UK, ranging from €1,000 to €20,000 per year.

The UK and EU have not reached an agreement on the issue, but the joint statement says the two sides will continue working towards a deal and conclude negotiations by May 2027.

The two sides have also agreed to continue discussions about the UK's participation in the Erasmus + programme.

The initiative provides funding for students, teachers, youth workers and sports professionals to study or do work experience in the EU.

The UK left the scheme in 2020 but last year the government re-joined for the 2027/28 academic year only, making a £570m contribution to the scheme.

In the statement released on Friday, the EU and UK agreed to explore opportunities "beyond 2027".

What are the criticisms of the scheme?

Some UK politicians had argued that the youth mobility scheme would disadvantage young people in the UK.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said: "I don't think it's fair because it means that more young people are coming here to compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs."

Speaking in the House of Commons on Thursday, Reform UK's Suella Braverman asked: "Why...are the government proposing to open the doors to hundreds of thousands of young Europeans who will come here and work in our shops and restaurants?

"Is that not a total and utter betrayal of young people in this country?"

Defending the government, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden has argued that countries in the EU with greater freedom of movement than the UK had lower youth unemployment rates.

The Labour government has made tackling the large number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) a top priority.

Alan Milburn, in his government-commissioned report into Neets, expressed concern about an "over-dependence" on foreign labour in the last 20 years.

He said the recent fall in net migration had created "an opportunity for employers to reorientate back towards employing young people from their communities".
