stories.title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last
stories.summary: The prime minister is learning how tough EU negotiations can be - but it won't deter him from seeking closer ties.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 20 November 2026

Andy Burnham has hailed his deal with the EU as a "good day for Britain" and a "good day for Europe".

In the hours before the prime minister spoke, it had become, if nothing else, a confusing day.

That confusion was unleashed by an EU official who briefed reporters in the morning that implementing the new arrangements on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions would be contingent on the government agreeing within six months to cut university tuition fees for Europeans studying in Britain.

That was later qualified by others in the EU - and straightforwardly disputed by the British government.

And for all that it dominated the morning, it did not ultimately dominate or particularly overshadow what was a warm press conference between the prime minister and his EU counterparts, Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa.

The settled position appears to be that negotiations on student fees will continue into the next six months but on a separate track, or a "different sheet of paper" as von der Leyen put it.

This still carries some degree of political risk for Burnham, because if Britain agrees to reduce, let alone equalise, university fees that would be an economic hit for universities which would presumably end up being covered by the government.

And it may still be possible, though probably unlikely, that a deterioration in those negotiations could pollute the progress of today's agreements.

Conversely, expect Burnham and his ministers to talk up another area where negotiations will continue - on the UK not being affected by the EU's "Made in Europe" plans, an attempt by the bloc to protect its industries from Chinese competition.

Today's achievements and hiccups alike may quickly pale into insignificance anyway.

UK and EU agree new deal for food exports, youth mobility and emissions but student fee talks to continue

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow Published 1 day ago

What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start? Published 1 day ago

At the dramatic conclusion of his first party conference speech as Labour leader in September - a moment he has been dreaming of for decades - the prime minister vowed to get closer to the EU.

Over the subsequent two months it has at times been a bit unclear how exactly he envisages that playing out and quite how far he is willing to go.

But focusing on the process risks obscuring the most important development, which is that the prime minister and the government are now unambiguously committed to Britain not only getting closer, but getting much closer to the EU.

There were two significant moments at today's summit in that regard.

First, Burnham said that the government had got as far as it could go with incremental deals with the EU, at least this side of a general election.

In other words, he has got as far as he believes is possible with the strategy he inherited from Sir Keir Starmer of getting closer to the EU within the confines of the post-Brexit architecture set out by Theresa May all those years ago, of Britain remaining outside the single market and the customs union.

That suggests that after two years of this, there will not be a third annual summit to unveil specific agreements designed to smooth post-Brexit issues affecting specific sectors.

Yet it does sound like there will be another summit next year - or, rather, an "informal brainstorming process" about potential options for future relations with the EU.

That sounds pretty nebulous, sure, but an event dedicated specifically to both sides discussing how to change the terms of Britain's arrangements with the EU is likely to become quite a big moment when it arrives.

Perhaps as importantly, von der Leyen made clear that the EU was embracing this event too.

That said, it does diminish the chances of major movement from Burnham towards embracing a specific model for the EU relationship in the intervening period.

And what of the domestic politics of this?

Britain's seventh prime minister in just over 10 years watched from Manchester as the fraught relationship with Europe wrecked the careers of so many of those predecessors.

Burnham's gamble is that this time it's different.

He believes that public regret about how Brexit has played out opens the political space for a far-reaching renegotiation.

Plenty of Labour MPs enthusiastically agree, and see this as the route to uniting the "progressive" vote at the next election too.

Some, especially those who represent Labour's former industrial heartlands, are a little more apprehensive.

This morning's confusion is a reminder that there is another element to this gamble.

Negotiating with Brussels, even if both sides believe progress is a "win-win", can be a fraught and complicated business.

Once he's on the other side of his brainstorm, can Burnham carry that off without getting bogged down and distracting from his government's other priorities?

On the day he became Labour leader in July, Burnham described it as the biggest change moment in British politics in 40 years.

He was talking principally about economic transformation.

But going to Brussels and getting what he wants without serious complications would be a pretty big change too.

stories.title: What does the new Brexit deal mean for Northern Ireland?
stories.summary: The agreement is expected to be confirmed when Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen meet in Brussels.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 20 November 2026

A new deal between the UK and the EU on food, plants and animals will "make a real positive difference for consumers, businesses and farmers" in Northern Ireland Stormont's agriculture minister has said.

The agreement was confirmed on Friday afternoon when Prime Minister Andy Burnham met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels.

Since Brexit, Northern Ireland has continued to follow EU rules for agri-food products while the rest of the UK has not.

The new deal will see the whole UK realigning with EU rules on those products, meaning goods being sent from GB to NI will no longer need to be checked at ports.

It will also mean a reduction but not elimination of the paperwork required to move agri-food goods from Great Britain to Northern Ireland.

The intention is to implement the deal from March 2028, though that could be dependent on the UK agreeing to reduce tuition fees for EU students.

Agriculture Minister Andrew Muir said "whilst this will not fix everything, it's a massive step in the right direction"

The minister Andrew Muir, said: "Whilst this will not fix everything, it's a massive step in the right direction.

"There will be huge benefits for all of us in Northern Ireland from reduced trade barriers and less checks on goods moving between GB to Northern Ireland.

"This will mean lower administrative hurdles and costs for businesses and government, as well as making it easier for retails to put produce on our shelves."

The UK and EU have also indicated a willingness to continue to jointly funding cross-border peace building projects in NI.

They say they will "explore the development of the successor programme" to the PeacePlus scheme which will end next year.

How does this impact the Irish Sea border?

Many unionists have been opposed the Irish Sea border

The Irish Sea border refers to checks and controls on goods entering Northern Ireland from the rest of the UK.

It came about as the result of a Brexit deal between the EU and UK in 2019. The deal was revised in 2023 and is now known as the Windsor Framework.

It was agreed that the most practical way to keep the border open between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland after Brexit was for Northern Ireland to follow EU laws on the regulation of goods.

However that means that goods coming from the rest of the UK into Northern Ireland face paperwork and other restrictions to ensure they meet EU standards.

Food products and plants face the most bureaucracy and this continues to cause problems for retailers.

For many nationalists in Northern Ireland, this has been a necessary compromise to minimise the impact of Brexit on the island of Ireland.

For many unionists it is a constitutional affront which undermines Northern Ireland's place in the UK.

The largest unionist party, the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), prevented Northern Ireland's power-sharing government from operating between 2022 and 2024 in protest at the sea border.

How should an agri-food deal change things?

Switzerland's borders with the EU illustrate what should change.

Like the UK Switzerland is not a member of the EU but there are no regulatory border controls for trade in agri-food products between Switzerland and the EU.

That is because the Swiss agreed to follow EU rules almost to the letter, without much say in setting those rules.

Switzerland is obliged to modify its laws in response to changes in EU legislation, what is known as dynamic alignment, and accept oversight from the European Court of Justice.

It is a Swiss-style deal which the UK and EU have agreed.

It will mean the sea-border controls on Great Britain food products entering Northern Ireland should be effectively ended from 2028.

Border control posts built at Northern Ireland ports should become largely redundant, although pre-Brexit checks on livestock would continue.

The "Not for EU" labels seen on Great Britain food products sold in Northern Ireland will no longer be needed.

What border processes would remain?

The Irish Sea is really two borders.

One deals with products' standards - making sure goods can be legally sold.

The other deals with customs - making sure the correct tariffs have been paid.

An agri-food deal should go a long way to removing the standards border but the new deal leaves the customs border untouched.

Businesses in Great Britain will still have to make customs declarations for goods going to Northern Ireland with the risk that goods would be delayed if the paperwork is incorrect.

What isn't in the deal?

A deal on electricity, which could cut costs for Northern Ireland consumers, was not part of this agreement.

There had been speculation that a "recoupling" of the EU and UK electricity grids would form part of the package.

Northern Ireland's energy regulator has said such a move could reduce wholesale electricity prices in Northern Ireland by up to 20%.

An electricity deal remains under negotiation, but the EU said it would need to include a financial contribution from the UK.

In a joint statement the EU and UK said: "We commit to conclude these negotiations in 2027, subject to final agreement by both parties, in order for all the necessary arrangements to take effect as soon as possible."

stories.body:
No breakthroughs on major subjects at first trilateral summit between leaders of US, China and Russia

T he presidents of the US, China and Russia met on Thursday for an unprecedented trilateral gathering on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen. The session lasted more than an hour and Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin touched on nuclear weapons, the war in Ukraine and wider international security.

The trio lead the world’s three major nuclear powers and their decisions have far-reaching consequences for global security. However, their meeting in China ended without an announced breakthrough or concrete agreement on the main issues. Here are five key takeaways:

Trump declared the meeting ‘historic’

Trump opened the talks by telling Xi and Putin that “we are really making history”. He described the US, China and Russia as “uniquely positioned” to discuss reducing their nuclear stockpiles and lowering the risk of such weapons being used.

It was an unusually high-profile display of cooperation between three countries whose relations have been marked by significant tensions, especially over Ukraine, trade disputes and the Nvidia scandal .

Trump also argued that peace could not be achieved by turning down opportunities for dialogue. It was the first time the leaders of the three countries had held a trilateral summit of this kind.

Nuclear arms control was a central issue

The talks came against the backdrop of the New Start nuclear agreement expiring in February . The treaty limits the arsenals of the US and Russia, capping each side at 1,550 deployed strategic nuclear warheads.

In September last year, Putin proposed voluntarily maintaining these limits for another year, but Trump rejected that approach, calling instead for a new agreement that would include China.

In the meeting on Thursday, Xi called for every effort to be made to prevent nuclear war and for nuclear weapons to be “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed”. However, no new arms control agreement was announced.

Ukraine was raised, without a breakthrough

Putin told Trump and Xi that their countries had “many converging interests” when it came to resolving conflicts, explicitly mentioning the war in Ukraine. He also spoke of their shared responsibility for international peace and security.

Like Putin, Trump arrived at the meeting fighting a failing war of choice. The Iran conflict has become an increasingly uncertain and costly undertaking for the US with no clear end in sight, while Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year, continues to exact a heavy toll.

The meeting offered little indication of progress toward ending the war in Ukraine, and Kyiv was not mentioned in the subsequent joint peace declaration.

Trump attacked the international criminal court

Trump described the international criminal court as “out of control”, criticising what he regards as the court’s excessive overreach.

His remarks carry particular significance given that Putin is wanted by the ICC on charges of war crimes. The court issued an arrest warrant for the Russian president in March 2023, accusing him of unlawfully deporting and transferring Ukrainian children from occupied territories to Russia.

The US and China are not signatories to the Rome statute, the international treaty that established the court, and are not bound by a requirement for member states to carry out its arrest warrants.

A joint ‘peace declaration’ was issued

A joint “peace declaration” issued after the meeting by Chinese and Russian state media called for UN reform “so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”.

The statement said the shake-up would range from boosting fuel supplies to engaging in “dialogue to reduce nuclear risks”.

The US and China are already permanent members of the UN security council, each with veto powers. They, and Russia, have argued for a greater role for nations from Asia, Africa and South America.

Russia has openly opposed permanent security council bids from Germany and Japan , arguing that western and Nato countries are already overrepresented and vote as a single bloc against Russian interests.

The declaration also took aim at the ICC, saying the court and similar bodies “must not abuse their jurisdiction”. It emphasised state consent and respect for the immunity of officials, which could be interpreted as a challenge to the legal basis for the ICC’s arrest warrant for Putin.

stories.title: Stabbed councillor 'protecting staff member during street clean'
stories.summary: Bradford councillor Ibrar Ali remains in hospital in a stable condition after he was stabbed.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Councillor Ibrar Ali is well known locally for community work

Published 20 November 2026

A councillor was trying to protect a member of council staff when he was stabbed while doing community work in his ward, his family has said.

Councillor Ibrar Ali remains in hospital in a stable condition after he was attacked at about 11:04 GMT on Thursday on Thornbury Avenue, before being driven to nearby Manse Street, according to police.

A 32-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after a stand-off on the roof of a home on Thornbury Avenue that lasted more than three hours. He remains in custody.

A statement on behalf of the independent councillor's family said he had intervened to protect a council staff member and "sustained multiple stab wounds".

Ali was doing street cleaning with Bradford Council staff when the incident happened.

The family statement continued: "Alhamdulillah [praise be to God], although his injuries are serious, they are not life-threatening. He is currently receiving treatment in hospital and remains in a stable condition.

"The family would like to express their heartfelt gratitude to everyone who has offered prayers, kind words and messages of support during this difficult time," they said.

The family thanked police, paramedics and members of the public who "courageously provided first aid and assistance at the scene" and said asked members of the public to "keep him and his family in your duas [prayers]".

"The family kindly requests privacy and understanding to allow Councillor Ibrar the time and space he needs to rest, heal and recover," it said.

Councillor Ibrar Ali was stabbed while undertaking community work in Bradford Moor

Ali is a Your Bradford Independent Group councillor for Bradford Moor ward and was first elected in May.

He works as a community development manager at charity The Leap, and was one of the founders of Leeds Road Festival.

Earlier West Yorkshire Police said there was "no information to suggest that this is a politically motivated incident at this time".

A spokesperson for Your Bradford Independent Group said they were "deeply shocked and concerned" by the stabbing.

"Such an attack is completely unacceptable. Violence has no place in our communities, and nobody should have to fear for their safety while carrying out their duties or going about their daily lives.

"Councillors dedicate their time to representing residents, supporting communities and making a difference to people's lives. Their safety and wellbeing must be taken seriously," they said.

Robert Jenrick will contest the seat he has held since 2024

Published 20 November 2026

MP Robert Jenrick has been reselected as Reform UK's candidate for the Newark seat in the next general election.

Jenrick had represented the Nottinghamshire constituency as a Conservative MP from 2014, before joining Reform in January this year.

There had been recent speculation that Jenrick would attempt to move to another seat , external for the next election, although he had previously said he intended to stand again in Newark.

On Friday, Reform's economic spokesman confirmed he had been reselected by his party to fight to keep his seat.

A Reform UK spokesperson said: "Robert is a formidable campaigner and one of the most hardworking MPs in Britain.

"He only got re-elected in 2024, against the odds, because of strength of support he has in the community.

"He has a deep connection with the people he represents, and we know he will continue to be a powerful voice for Newark and one of the most influential politicians in Britain."

Jenrick was sacked by Kemi Badenoch for plotting to defect to Nigel Farage's party hours before the official announcement by Reform in January.

He was first elected in a by-election to the Nottinghamshire seat in in 2014, with a majority of 7,400 votes.

In 2024, Jenrick held the seat as as a Tory, with a majority of just over 3,500 votes.

His defection earlier this year meant it was the first time Nottinghamshire had no Conservative representation in Parliament since 1970.

Last week, the Conservatives selected former Sherwood MP Sir Mark Spencer to contest the Newark seat.

Spender was the MP for Sherwood for 14 years but lost his seat to Labour at the last general election.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’

China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.

The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.

The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.

The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.

“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”

Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.

Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.

The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.

“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.

Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.

In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.

First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”

The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.

Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”

Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .

Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.

European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.

The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.

Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.

Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.

Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

stories.summary: The scheme is expected to be approved at Friday's UK-EU summit, with new deals on food trade and carbon emissions also on the table.

Watch: Burnham says he wants 'best deal for Britain' at UK-EU summit

Published 19 November 2026

Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agreed on Friday, the BBC understands.

The same number of young Britons would be allowed into Europe under the scheme, expected to be approved at the UK-EU summit in Brussels. Downing Street has not commented on the details, but said talks were "down to the wire" on Thursday.

The prime minister has said a "Channel action plan" on immigration could also be struck, while negotiators are seeking agreements on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions" of the Brexit referendum.

A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.

The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.

In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.

Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal - arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.

Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.

The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in negotiation ahead of the summit, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.

Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from a deal on Friday.

"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.

"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.

"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."

Burnham previously said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.

The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal were secured, the government would introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.

The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next Published 2 days ago

Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs? Published 5 days ago

The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left Published 3 days ago

An agreement on trade could remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.

The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.

However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling.

Burnham has also said the summit would allow the UK to raise concerns about the Made in Europe scheme, which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.

Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.

The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.

Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU.

However, the subject has divided his cabinet with one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, speaking to The Sun , external , said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU.

He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Thursday, Badenoch said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but "not trade at any cost".

She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc.

Appearing on BBC Breakfast on Friday, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage described the agreement as a "very, very expensive and costly error" and said Burnham has no "democratic mandate to do any of this".

He added that the Labour party manifesto was clear that the UK would not go back towards the single market and asked: "Where is our democracy?".

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey told BBC Newsnight that while he agreed with Burnham on "the harms of Brexit", he did not think the prime minister was "going to go anywhere near far enough".

"We need to go further and faster," he said, including returning to freedom of movement - which Sir Ed said would help tackle immigration and boost the UK economy.

stories.title: Fine Gael leader wants border poll criteria talks with London
stories.summary: Simon Harris says a conversation between the British and Irish governments over the criteria for a border poll would be "useful".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Simon Harris is due to become taoiseach in November 2027

Published 19 November 2026

The leader of Fine Gael, Simon Harris, has said that a conversation between the British and Irish governments over the criteria for a border poll would be "useful".

Harris, who is the tánaiste (Irish deputy prime minister), said he and the Taoiseach (Irish PM) Micheál Martin are "aligned" on the issue.

He said there could be joint Irish government proposals on Irish unity preparation "by the end of the year".

It comes after the Northern Ireland Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said that it is his job to decide when to bring forward a border poll and that he does not "detect a mood" for it.

Harris said that it would be good if the British and Irish governments "could at least have a shared understanding as to what criteria may be considered".

"At a point in time Dublin and London having a conversation about criteria is useful and is also just good governance," he said

Speaking on BBC News NI's The View programme, he added: "British Irish relations have never been better".

Under the Good Friday Agreement, Bryant as the NI Secretary of State, decides whether to call a border poll or not.

On Thursday morning Sir Chris told RTÉ's Morning Ireland programme , external he would "only bring forward a border poll at such time" as he thinks the people of Northern Ireland would want to join a united Ireland

"I don't detect that that is the situation now," he added.

Asked what criteria he will use to decide if the mood to join a united Ireland appears likely, he said "when it appears likely".

Under the Good Friday Agreement, Bryant as the NI Secretary of State decides whether to call a border poll or not

When asked why the Irish government should not have a role, Sir Chris said that the Good Friday Agreement is very clear that it's a matter for the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland and that is agreed by the two governments as co-guarantors.

In response, the tánaiste said that "the commitment in the Good Friday Agreement is exactly as Chris Bryant read out, there's no disputing of that. But the application of that is something that would be good to have a greater understanding".

Simon Harris sent a letter to some party leaders in Northern Ireland asking for their views after his party, Fine Gael, published proposals on how to prepare for Irish unity .

The "blueprint" on Irish unity came days after the taoiseach, leader of Fianna Fáil, circulated a document to his parliamentary party laying out his own thoughts on how to prepare for a united Ireland .

He proposed setting up a new "initiative" on the constitutional future of the island of Ireland.

The two parties are both in a coalition government, supported by a number of Independent TDs (members of the Irish parliament) in Dublin.

Simon Harris is due to become taoiseach in November 2027, under the coalition's rotating taoiseach agreement.

He added that he had already had discussions with the Taoiseach Micheál Martin.

'Equal' constitutional futures

Harris said that people don't need to agree with the outcome to wish to partake in discussions on Irish unity.

"We no longer live on an island where one constitutional view has greater value than the other. We left that behind us as a people when we voted for the Good Friday Agreement,"he said.

"Both views are legitimate and just like nationalists have lived in a Northern Ireland that has been part of the United Kingdom, it is possible in the future that unionists will live in a Northern Ireland that is part of a united Ireland."

"In both scenarios it's important that we have good relations. It's important that we are respectful, inclusive and we are willing to engage."

What's in Harris' 'blueprint'?

Among their proposals, Fine Gael has suggested appointing a junior minister in the Irish government for "north south relations".

The party also published a document by an economist who works as an adviser to Harris, where it was suggested that the first-year cost of reunification ranges from about €3bn (£2.5bn) to €25bn (£20.8bn) to the Irish exchequer.

His party has now proposed setting up an "independent, government-supported, inter-party and consultative forum" as part of preparations for reunification of the island.

The forum would look at the "future" of the institutions in Northern Ireland and the "possible subsequent reform of local and regional government on an all-island basis in line with the European principle of subsidiarity".

It would also examine the changes needed in Ireland's institutions, as well as public taxation, healthcare, education and other public services and practical requirements.

What has the political reaction been?

Sinn Féin First Minister Michelle O'Neill said she welcomed the tánaiste's call for clarity on the criteria for a referendum on Irish unity adding "the British Government cannot continue to ignore the historic change on our island".

Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson said that his party was "not interested in self-harm and conversations that would see the end of the UK as we know it".

Alliance leader Naomi Long has said that her party will "engage respectfully" in any conversations about Northern Ireland's future.

The SDLP leader Claire Hanna welcomed the letter and said "a New Ireland must mean precisely that: an opportunity to build a new nation, not simply reverse partition".

Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader Jon Burrows, described Fine Gael's plans as a "constitutional pet project" and said his party "will not participate in any project designed to dismantle the United Kingdom".

In his response to Harris, Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister said his "courtship techniques are somewhat lacking".

In response to unionist concerns, Harris said that "they are absolutely entitled to disagree" but that he "would never call their view in relation to the constitutional status fairy-tale or dangerous and all I would ask in respectful debate that they would too".

Analysis

Simon Harris may have stopped short of demanding the British government publish the criteria for a border poll but this is a nudge in that direction.

He, like his partner in government Michael Martin, is keen to flush out what the threshold for a poll might look like.

But they know there is little chance of that happening anytime soon.

Setting out the criteria for a border poll would result in the British government surrendering control of the process and that is something it is not prepared to do.

There is no desire to be tied to a threshold beyond its control.

So while unionists will argue this latest Harris intervention hasn't brought the prospect of a united Ireland any closer, it has injected more momentum into the wider unity conversation.

And the prospect now of a joint Dublin government proposal on Irish unity will energise the debate even more.

The Taoiseach and Tánaiste are no longer spectators in the stand, they are now players on the pitch and it feels like game on.

stories.body:
US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake

Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.

The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.

Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump , California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway .

White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.

“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.

“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.

Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.

Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep . Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.

“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.

Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.

“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News .

Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health , often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

Far from the grand ambitions declared in Yalta in 1945, Shenzhen felt like a meeting in search of an agenda

It is arguably true, given it was the first such meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US, that Thursday’s gathering in Shenzhen deserved the description of “historic”.

But in terms of tangible outcomes, it is unlikely to warrant the “new page in the history of diplomacy” that Vladimir Putin claimed had been written, and will instead be consigned to a smallish footnote in any future volume of the 21st century.

It’s true that the meeting could yet be an icebreaker and the start of a permanent new dialogue. It’s also true that each leader can return home with something from the 90 minutes they spent together.

Despite falling asleep during the main Apec summit, Donald Trump had a chance to show his proximity to two authoritarian leaders he admires. With Ukraine having destroyed Russia’s bridge into Crimea , the US president greeted Putin as not just a friend but almost a wartime ally.

The Russian president, although occasionally pushed to one side by protocol during the early photo opportunities, will be able to show back home that it is Moscow, and not his adversary Europe, let alone Ukraine, that commands the respect and attention of Trump and Xi Jinping . As such, the summit was a free gift to Putin, and underlined that Trump was no longer the leader of the free world, as the former British foreign secretary Jeremy Hunt commented.

From Putin’s perspective, a meeting in Berlin of the coalition of the willing was a sideshow. Europe’s attempts to isolate Russia had failed and the Asia-Pacific region had become the centre of the global economy, Putin boasted. His relationship with Trump, he said, despite the difficulties, was founded on “similar civilisational values”.

For Xi, it was a prestigious chance to play host and implicitly demonstrate that the era of American hegemony is over. No longer the sole arbiter in world affairs, the US, the consumer economy, must share the stage with China , the manufacturing giant, and Russia, the energy bank.

The trio’s brief joint statement covered four pretty disparate topics: boosting energy supply, reforming the United Nations, limiting the powers of the international criminal court (ICC) and a tentative commitment to discuss nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation.

For grandeur at a time of various global crises, these ambitions hardly matched Yalta in 1945 or even the declaration after the Tehran summit in 1943, when the leaders of the UK, US and the USSR sat on the veranda of the British embassy and pledged that their countries would work together after the war to build a “world family of democratic nations” free of tyranny and oppression. Winston Churchill declaimed in Tehran: “In our hands we have the future of mankind.” Joseph Stalin went further. “History has spoiled us,” he said. “She has given us very great power and very great opportunities.”

Shenzhen, by contrast, felt like a meeting in search of an agenda. The vacuum was filled with platitudinous commitments to “maintain strategic stability and international security”, a task that – looking around the world – none of those in attendance are currently pursuing with great effect.

Perhaps technology, multipolarity and their own divisions mean even they do not have “very great power”. Certainly there were no accompanying plans for how to reform the UN, let alone boost energy production or show respect for international law – a subject Trump’s current favoured successor, Marco Rubio, had just disparaged in a speech as a plaything of the global elite.

It was the summit’s chief instigator, Putin, who was the most eager of the three to set the meeting in a historic context, describing China, Russia and the US as the victors of the second world war, in a deliberate slight to Britain. A pledge to “preserve and strengthen the system of international law” seemingly referred to ensuring certain world leaders were freed from the prospect of the ICC serving them with arrest warrants.

By coincidence, the other world court, the international court of justice (ICJ), found a state – Myanmar – guilty of genocide for the first time on the same day. The Shenzen statement did not name the ICJ as a target, beyond an oblique reference to the ICC and “other similar institutions”. Doubtless that is only because ICJ rulings can be dismissed with near impunity.

Xi, nervous that China’s status as protector of the global south might be damaged by being involved in a global superpower carve-up, stuck to a familiar script: “History tells us that when major powers are at peace, the world is secure. When they clash, there is chaos.”

It may be that behind the scenes, or at other events, serious progress is being made on how China might act as a guarantor of a peace deal with Iran, or on who should lead the UN through its coming phase of reform, or even on how Putin might bring himself to seek peace in Ukraine in a way that protects Ukrainian sovereignty.

For the moment, though, it looks as if what little history was made in Shenzhen was made for exclusively the wrong reasons.

The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout

Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?

As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.

Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.

Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.

US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap.

Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”

Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.

The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.

European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.

The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO .

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.

“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.

Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”

Nvidia shares fell byafter California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.

Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.

Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

Kristalina Georgieva says countries needed to be ready for tech rollout, adding: ‘You snooze, you lose’

Business live – latest updates

Booming demand for artificial intelligence will force the world’s most powerful central banks to raise interest rates, the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned.

Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the Washington-based fund, said demand for AI hardware and related technology products was pushing up consumer prices around the world.

She said that, alongside the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, this was adding to inflationary pressures around the globe.

“This calls for a tightening of monetary policy in many economies,” she said.

Speaking at the 2026 Apec summit in Shenzhen , Georgieva warned that both factors would push global inflation to 4.7% this year. She added that the rapid rollout of AI was also contributing to stronger than expected economic growth in several countries, despite the headwinds from the Iran war.

Central banks have been forced to raise interest rates this year after the outbreak of war in February drove the global oil price above $100 a barrel, reigniting inflationary pressures around the world. The European Central Bank (ECB) raised rates in June for the first time since 2023, followed by the US Federal Reserve in September and the Bank of England earlier this month .

Financial markets expect further increases in the cost of borrowing next year, as the rapid rollout of AI bolsters economic growth against the volatile backdrop of the conflict.

However, global oil prices have fallen back in recent weeks, following the US midterm elections and an upswing in the supply of crude . Fears about an AI bubble and febrile conditions in global equity markets could dent business investment, and economists warn of a slowdown in demand as high inflation squeezes households.

Georgieva said that while the energy shock would eventually dissipate, “AI is for ever” – making it a significant driver of world trade, competitiveness, productivity and economic growth.

AI hardware and related tech products now account for more than one-tenth of the world goods trade, a share that is rapidly rising, she said. But some countries were benefiting more from investment than others.

“To put it simply: you snooze, you lose,” she added. “Countries need digital infrastructure, labour markets and workers that are ready for AI, and risk mitigation – especially to control financial stability and cybersecurity risks.”

after newsletter promotion

Georgieva’s comments came a day after the ECB expressed concerns about the rising amount of debt that AI companies are taking on to fuel their growth.

The central bank said there were “historic parallels” with the dotcom bubble that led to a tech market crash at the turn of the millennium, as well as the sub-prime mortgage bubble that set off the 2008 financial crisis. It said in its financial stability review that any fallout from an AI crash “could lead to spillovers affecting euro-area financial stability”.

For now, at least, the sector is still booming. Thursday marked a pivotal day for AI as Anthropic debuted on the US stock market , raising the largest investment of any initial public offering after pricing at $83 per share.

The company, which makes the AI chatbot Claude, is expected to become one of the most valuable publicly traded businesses in the world at $1.5tn, despite reporting losses of $80bn in the first half of 2026.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A handful of men control the US economy. They have leveraged themselves to be – or seem – indispensable

Jensen Huang has said he would return to Nvidia as its CEO if its board requests it.

“I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said . “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

Huang, who admitted being unfaithful to his wife, resigned from Nvidia last week. US intelligence agencies have identified one of his alleged lovers as a spy for China. If true, Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips may have found their way there.

Beyond the tabloid headlines lies a much bigger story – a US economy that’s become dependent on the initiatives and decisions of a few powerful men who are too big to fail.

We tend to think of government as being authoritarian, democratic or somewhere in between. For the last 22 months, we’ve witnessed what happens when the US government turns authoritarian.

An economy can also be described along the same continuum.

Throughout most of the last century, the US economy was fairly democratic. Decisions about what was produced and at what price reflected the judgments of tens of thousands of corporate executives, managers and small-business owners – all of whom were trying to respond to consumers and investors. Through labor unions, workers also had some say.

But the US economy has become far more authoritarian.

In recent decades, it’s become concentrated in the hands of a few giant corporations. Economies of scale have enabled those corporations to spread their fixed costs over many goods and services, and the US government has nearly abandoned antitrust (anti-monopoly) enforcement.

Labor unions have shrunk from representing over a third of private-sector workers in the 1950s to just 6% today.

More recently – over the last five years – something else has occurred, especially in big tech, that’s pushed the economy much further toward authoritarianism.

A handful of men – among them, Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg, Larry Ellison, Tim Cook and Jensen Huang – have not only become the richest people in the world, with significant political clout. They also control the direction and pace of technologies on which the US and the world depend.

These men are, in fact, the authoritarians of the new economy. They have unparalleled power over every aspect of the lives of Americans and millions of others around the world. And they have leveraged themselves to be, or seem, too big to fail.

The leverage works like this.

Nvidia’s value depends on Jensen Huang.

Hours after Huang’s resignation last Thursday, Nvidia stock dropped 10.3% in pre-market trading, erasing approximately $490bn of Nvidia’s value by the time the market opened.

Since the start of the leadership controversy at Nvidia on 8 November, the company has lost about $800bn in market value.

The AI industry, in turn, depends on Nvidia. Nvidia controls about 90% of the global market share of advanced AI chips. It has also become the major financier for the entire AI industry. Some call Nvidia the “ central bank of AI ”.

Nvidia’s $5tn market value (before 8 November) equaled about 8% of the total value of the S&P 500.

The US economy, in turn, depends on the AI industry. In the first quarter of 2025, the buildouts of datacenters using Nvidia chips accounted for 92% of US economic growth. Over the past two years, AI has been responsible for roughly half of America’s overall growth.

This huge leverage also works in reverse. Analysts fear that Nvidia’s collapse could cause the AI bubble to burst, triggering a failure that could threaten the entire US, if not also the world, economy.

Most Americans’ 401(k)s are invested in giant index funds tied to the Nasdaq and S&P 500. The Nasdaq and S&P 500, in turn, are based largely on 10 huge corporations . These 10 corporations are all connected to Nvidia. Together, they comprise about 37% of the value of the entire US stock market.

What all this means is Jensen Huang may be too big to fail.

More than 177,000 people have so far signed a “Stand with Jensen” open letter demanding that Nvidia’s board of directors “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”. Signers include Elon Musk; the Y Combinator president, Garry Tan; the Epic Games CEO, Tim Sweeney; and thousands of self-reported Nvidia employees.

Huang is discussing a possible return to the company, though the chair of the company’s board has said it’s not considering the move . One Huang ally talks of a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia ‌CEO’s return, ‌and garner support from ‌Trump. “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person told the Financial Times, adding that the efforts have Huang’s support.

Trump told reporters on Monday that he “would not mind” if Huang were reinstated as Nvidia CEO, adding that he thought Huang had “learned a big lesson”.

Exactly what “big lesson” did Trump have in mind? That it’s not a good look for the CEO of the US’s most valuable corporation to have a romantic relationship out of wedlock?

Or that such a CEO shouldn’t break the law by supplying America’s most advanced AI chips to China through a Chinese spy?

On Tuesday, it was announced that Huang has agreed to appear on 1 December before the House foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party and the House intelligence committee in transcribed interviews.

Even in an authoritarian economy, no CEO is above the law. Or is he? We may soon find out.

Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com . His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

A trilateral gathering is good news for China and Russia, but bad for the US – and its traditional allies

“H istoric” is a neutral descriptor, not a favourable one. Things can be unprecedented for good reason. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Thursday will be the first time that the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio. The trilateral on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is striking, but it is not an achievement.

The lack of a clear agenda is telling: the spectacle really is the substance. Mr Trump sees international affairs in terms of spheres of influence. This meeting reinforces the obvious conclusion for the rest of the world – that they don’t get to sit at the table, only to be on the plate. Mr Xi promotes the notion of a multipolar world. Others would be more sympathetic if all three governments were not determinedly undermining multilateralism.

Mr Xi looks like the power broker bringing Moscow and Washington together, and the gracious host, in a city which showcases China’s economic and technological progress and aspirations. The contrast between the glossy metropolis and a US currently beset by glaring tech failures hitting everything from flights to banking is especially flattering. For Mr Putin, who gloated about the “humiliation” of Europe in the run-up, this meeting is an even clearer win, making him look like a superpower peer rather than the leader of a pariah nation with a struggling economy.

Mr Trump has got a red carpet embrace, another “first” to promote – preferable to headlines dwelling on the Republicans’ midterms disaster – and the congenial company of strongmen. His nation has less to celebrate. Mr Trump seems to see meeting longstanding US allies as at best a chore. His bruising tariffs and nakedly transactional approach to security, as well as his love of autocrats, have pushed countries like the Philippines – which hosted the US president en route to China – into hedging their bets.

Mr Trump is not expected to raise Nvidia and suspected Chinese espionage – perhaps not least because his closeness to Jensen Huang, the company’s ousted CEO, makes the issue at least as discomfiting for him as it is for Beijing. The US president is unlikely to embarrass the two countries that are central to Iran’s ability to resist his disastrous and illegal war, or to press China over its facilitation of Russia’s war against Ukraine . Ukraine and Taiwan have reason to be anxious any time he speaks to Mr Putin and Mr Xi. But the US president is as likely to undermine them, whether deliberately or otherwise, in bilaterals or via a throwaway remark.

Comparisons to the 1945 Yalta summit of Joseph Stalin, Franklin D Roosevelt and Winston Churchill – which divided up Europe – grotesquely overstate the importance of a meeting scheduled to last less than an hour. Mr Xi does not do spontaneity, and is unlikely to be lured into sudden announcements. And despite the surface amity, the three still have strongly competing interests. China’s threat to rare earths brought a trade truce, but skirmishes continue. Mr Trump has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation . While China is arming itself at worrying speed, its arsenal is still dwarfed by those of the US and Russia.

Talking to rivals and adversaries is not inherently unwise. Under another US president, a closely focused and carefully prepared trilateral on, for instance, disarmament might even be fruitful. This is not that world. This will not be that meeting.
